course.title: Electrical: How Power Gets to Your Outlets
course.lead: A free, self-paced course on the electrical system of a home: where the power comes from, how the panel, circuits and outlets work, how grounding, GFCIs and AFCIs keep you safe, how to tell when something’s wrong, what you can safely do yourself, and when to call a licensed electrician.
course.who: Written for teens and adults with no electrical experience. It picks up where the electrical guides in Being an Adult 101 leave off.
course.why: Each lesson explains the “why” as well as the “what”: Ohm’s law and power, why the grid runs at high voltage, how a breaker’s bimetal and magnet tell an overload from a short, how a GFCI senses a few milliamps of leakage. Facts and numbers come from U.S. government agencies (OSHA, NIOSH, CPSC, the U.S. Fire Administration, the Department of Energy and its Energy Information Administration, and BLS), university programs and OpenStax physics textbooks, and every lesson lists its sources.
how: Start with Lesson 1 for the big picture, then go in order or jump to the part you’re curious about.
Each lesson has diagrams, a “parts and what they do” table, a short quiz and links to go deeper. Badges show the level.
Play with the interactive pieces: the power grid, the breaker, the kitchen circuit, the GFCI and the hallway switches.
Use the troubleshooting finder when something seems wrong, and climb the skill ladder one rung at a time.
course.final: Your local code and a licensed electrician are the final word. This course explains how home electrical systems work in general. Your state and local electrical codes, enforced by your local inspector (the authority having jurisdiction), decide what’s allowed where you live. Permits and inspections may be required, and much electrical work legally requires a licensed electrician. Follow the instructions that come with every device and appliance.

lessons.title: The Big Picture: From Power Plant to Outlet
lessons.short: Generation, high-voltage transmission, substations and transformers, distribution, the service, the meter, the panel and the circuits, with a map of the house.
lessons.intro: Flip a switch and the light comes on at once. Behind that switch is a chain of machines and wires that starts at a power plant, often far away. This lesson follows electricity from the plant to your outlet and gives you a map of the electrical system in a house. Every later lesson zooms in on one part of it.

blocks.h: It starts with a spinning magnet
blocks.html:
Most power plants make electricity with a generator. Moving a magnet inside a coil of wire makes an electric current flow in the wire. A power plant does the same thing on a giant scale: a turbine spins a magnet past coils of wire, and current flows.

What spins the turbine depends on the plant. In a turbine generator, a moving fluid (water, steam, hot combustion gases or air) pushes a series of blades. Steam comes from burning coal or natural gas or from a nuclear reactor; dams use falling water; wind turbines use the wind. Solar panels are the big exception: they make electricity straight from sunlight with no moving parts (Lesson 10).

In 2022, natural gas plants made about 40 percent of the electricity from large U.S. power plants, coal about 19 percent, nuclear about 18 percent, wind about 10 percent, hydropower about 6 percent and large solar plants about 3 percent.

Electricity travels from power plants to homes through a connected network of lines and equipment called the grid. The U.S. grid has thousands of miles of high-voltage power lines and millions of miles of low-voltage lines. Here’s the trip, step by step:

  1. Step up. Next to the power plant, transformers raise the voltage. For long-distance transmission it’s raised to over 200,000 volts (200 kilovolts, kV), sometimes as high as 700 kV.
  2. Transmission. High-voltage lines, the ones strung between tall metal towers, carry the power over long distances.
  3. Substation. Near the towns that use the power, transformers in substations step the voltage back down.
  4. Distribution. Lower-voltage lines run along streets on poles or underground, usually at 5 to 13 kV.
  5. The last transformer. A transformer on a pole or in a box on the ground drops the voltage to 120 and 240 volts for homes.
  6. The service. Wires run from that transformer to your house, overhead (the service drop) or underground. They pass through the electric meter and into your main panel, which splits the power into branch circuits for each part of the house.

Along the way, some energy turns into heat in the wires. The U.S. Energy Information Administration estimates that about 5 percent of the electricity sent out was lost in transmission and distribution in 2018 through 2022.

blocks.html:
Power is voltage times current: P = V × I. To send the same power, you can use high voltage and a small current, or low voltage and a big current. The wires don’t care about voltage, but they do care about current. A wire with resistance R wastes power as heat at a rate of I² × R. Double the current and you get four times the heat.

So the grid sends power at high voltage to keep the current small. The OpenStax physics textbook works an example: 100 megawatts sent at 200 kV needs only 500 amps, and through lines with 1 ohm of resistance it loses 250 kilowatts, just 0.25 percent. Send the same power at 25 kV and the current jumps to 4,000 amps, and the lines waste 16 megawatts, 16 percent of it. Try it below.

This is also why the grid uses alternating current (AC). Transformers can raise and lower AC voltages easily and efficiently, often better than 99 percent. Doing the same with direct current is much harder. You’ll see the math in Lesson 2.

blocks.cap: A simple model: the current in the line is the power sent divided by the voltage, and the heat lost is current squared times the line’s resistance. The starting values are OpenStax Example 20.10.

blocks.html:
Inside the house, the electrical system has a few main parts. The meter measures how much energy you use. The main panel holds the main breaker and a breaker for each circuit. Branch circuits carry power from the panel to outlets, switches, lights and appliances. Big appliances such as a dryer, range or water heater get their own 240-volt circuits. And a set of protective parts, the ground wires and grounding electrode, GFCIs, AFCIs and alarms, is there to keep people and the house safe when something goes wrong.

quiz.q: What does a power plant’s generator do?
opts: Turns motion into electricity by moving magnets past coils of wire
quiz.why: A turbine spins a magnet past coils of wire, and the changing magnetic field makes current flow.

quiz.q: Why is power sent over long distances at very high voltage?
opts: For the same power, the current is smaller, so much less is lost as heat in the wires
quiz.why: Power is V × I, and heat lost in a wire is I² × R. Higher voltage means less current and far less loss.

quiz.q: In the OpenStax example, how much of 100 MW is lost in 1-ohm lines at 25 kV instead of 200 kV?
quiz.why: At 25 kV the current is 4,000 A, and 4,000² × 1 Ω = 16 MW, which is 16 percent.

quiz.q: What is the service drop?
opts: The overhead wires from the utility’s last pole to your house
quiz.why: The service drop is the overhead service wiring from the utility’s pole to the building. Some homes get underground service instead.

quiz.q: About what share of U.S. electricity was lost in transmission and distribution in 2018 through 2022, according to EIA?
quiz.why: EIA estimates annual transmission and distribution losses at about 5 percent.

lessons.title: Volts, Amps, Ohms and Watts
lessons.short: Ohm’s law, power, kilowatt-hours and your bill, alternating current at 60 hertz, and 120/240-volt split-phase service.
lessons.intro: Four little words do most of the work in electricity: volts, amps, ohms and watts. Once you know how they fit together, you can read an appliance label, predict when a breaker will trip, and check your electric bill. This lesson gives you the formulas and the reasons behind them.

blocks.html:
Voltage, measured in volts (V), is the electrical push that makes charge move. Current, measured in amperes or amps (A), is how much charge flows past a point each second. Resistance, measured in ohms (Ω), is how hard the path is to push through. A thin wire, a long wire, or the glowing coil in a toaster has more resistance than a short, thick copper wire.

Ohm’s law ties the three together: voltage equals current times resistance. Flip it around and you can find any one from the other two. A heating element with 12 ohms of resistance, plugged into a 120-volt outlet, draws 120 ÷ 12 = 10 amps.
V = I × R  <small>(volts = amps × ohms, so I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I)</small>

blocks.h: Watts: how fast energy is used
blocks.html:
Power, measured in watts (W), is how fast a device uses energy. For any device, power is voltage times current. A kilowatt (kW) is 1,000 watts. For a simple heater, you can also write power as current squared times resistance, or voltage squared divided by resistance. That I²R form is the one that explains why wires get hot.

Most appliances list their watts on a label or nameplate, usually on the bottom or back. If the label gives only amps, multiply by the voltage: a 3-amp shredder on 120 volts uses 120 × 3 = 360 watts. Going the other way, a 1,500-watt electric kettle on 120 volts draws 1,500 ÷ 120 = 12.5 amps. That number matters when you share a circuit (Lesson 4).

P = V × I  (watts = volts × amps, so amps = watts ÷ volts)
P = I² × R = V² ÷ R  (for a resistor such as a heating element)

Your electric company doesn’t charge for watts. It charges for energy: power multiplied by time. The unit on your bill is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), one kilowatt used for one hour. A 40-watt bulb that’s on for five hours uses 200 watt-hours, or 0.2 kWh.

The U.S. Department of Energy gives a simple recipe: multiply an appliance’s watts by the hours you use it each day, then divide by 1,000 to get kWh per day. Multiply by the number of days, then by your price per kWh. A 1,500-watt kettle used one hour a day uses 1.5 kWh a day, or 547.5 kWh a year.

Prices vary from place to place. The U.S. average residential price was 18.31 cents per kWh in July 2026, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. At that price, the kettle costs about $100 a year to run. In 2022 the average U.S. home bought about 10,791 kWh of electricity, about 899 kWh a month. Try your own appliances below; your bill shows your actual price.

blocks.html:
A battery pushes current one way only: direct current (DC). The power at your outlets is alternating current (AC). The voltage swings from about +170 volts to −170 volts and back, 60 times every second (60 hertz, Hz), so the current keeps reversing direction.

Why call it 120 volts, then? Because a swinging voltage delivers the same average heating power as a steady voltage of its peak divided by √2. That “root mean square” value is 170 ÷ 1.414 ≈ 120 volts. When you see 120 or 240 volts for AC, that’s the rms value.
V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>peak</sub> ÷ √2  <small>(170 V ÷ 1.414 ≈ 120 V)</small>

blocks.h: 120 and 240 volts from the same service
blocks.html:
Most U.S. homes get “120/240-volt” service. Utilities try to hold 120/240 volts at the meter. The service has three main wires: two “hot” legs and a neutral. Each hot leg is 120 volts from the neutral, and the two hot legs are 240 volts from each other, because they swing in opposite directions. When one is at +170 volts, the other is at −170 volts.

Ordinary outlets and lights use one hot leg and the neutral: 120 volts. Big loads such as electric ranges, clothes dryers, water heaters and Level 2 electric-car chargers connect across both hot legs: 240 volts. The reason is the same one that drives the grid. For the same power, twice the voltage means half the current, and the wires waste a quarter as much heat. A 4,500-watt water heater draws 18.75 amps at 240 volts. At 120 volts it would need 37.5 amps.

blocks.cap: Ordinary outlets use one hot leg and the neutral (120 V). Dryers, ranges and water heaters use both hot legs (240 V). Sources: University of Hawaiʻi Maui College; University of Missouri Extension; OpenStax 20.5 for the ±170 V peaks.

blocks.html: A transformer is two coils of wire wound on an iron core. Alternating current in the first coil makes a changing magnetic field, and that field makes a voltage in the second coil. The voltage ratio equals the ratio of the number of turns. Because the power out nearly equals the power in, a transformer that raises the voltage lowers the current by the same ratio. Transformers need a changing current to work, which is a big reason the grid is AC: it’s much easier to raise and lower AC voltages than DC.
V<sub>s</sub> ÷ V<sub>p</sub> = N<sub>s</sub> ÷ N<sub>p</sub>  <small>(secondary to primary voltage = ratio of turns; power in ≈ power out)</small>

blocks.h: Why the breaker trips when the toaster and kettle run together
blocks.html: Each appliance on a circuit adds its own current. A 1,500-watt kettle draws 12.5 amps and a 1,100-watt toaster about 9.2 amps. Together that’s about 21.7 amps, more than a 20-amp breaker allows, so sooner or later it trips. Lesson 4 has a game where you can try it.

lessons.short: The service entrance, the meter, the main breaker, bus bars, how a breaker trips, fuses, neutral and ground bars, subpanels and service size.
lessons.intro: The main panel is the heart of a home’s electrical system. Power from the utility comes in through the meter, passes through the main breaker, and is split up into branch circuits, each guarded by its own breaker. This lesson explains every part and how a breaker knows when to trip. It isn’t a how-to: work inside a panel belongs with a licensed electrician.

blocks.h: The service: from the utility to the panel
blocks.html:
The “service” is the set of wires and equipment that brings electricity from the utility to a building’s wiring. With overhead service, the service drop runs from the utility’s last pole to the house. With underground service, the wires come up from a buried line instead. Either way, they reach the meter socket, which holds the utility’s meter, and continue to the service equipment: usually a main breaker, or switches and fuses in older homes.

The meter counts kilowatt-hours. Many newer meters send your usage to the utility wirelessly. The utility is generally responsible for the equipment from the service connection at your house back to its distribution lines.

A panel (the code calls it a panelboard) is a metal cabinet with a cover. Behind the cover are live parts, energized metal you must never touch:

  • The main breaker can switch off and protect everything at once. It’s sized for the home’s largest expected load.
  • Two hot bus bars are heavy metal strips, one for each 120-volt leg of the service. Breakers clip onto them.
  • Branch-circuit breakers each feed and protect one circuit. A single breaker connects one leg for 120 volts. A double-width breaker connects both legs for 240 volts, which is why a 240-volt circuit takes two breaker spaces.
  • The neutral bar is where the white neutral wires of the circuits end.
  • The ground bar collects the bare or green equipment ground wires. At the service, the neutral and the equipment grounds are tied to a grounding electrode, such as a rod in the earth, through the grounding electrode conductor (Lesson 5).

The card inside the panel door should say which breaker feeds which rooms. If yours is blank, Being an Adult 101 shows how to label it.

blocks.h: How a breaker knows when to trip
blocks.html:
A circuit breaker is a switch that opens itself when too much current flows. Most home breakers have two separate trip mechanisms, because there are two kinds of trouble.

Overloads trip the thermal element. Current through a bimetal strip, two metals bonded together that expand by different amounts, heats it, and the strip bends. Bend it far enough and it releases a latch, and a spring snaps the contacts apart. Heating depends on current squared multiplied by time, so a small overload takes a long time to trip and a big one is quick. The safety standard for breakers (UL 489, as described by CPSC staff) requires 15- and 20-amp breakers to trip within 2 minutes at 200 percent of their rating and within 1 hour at 135 percent. That delay is on purpose. Wires heat up gradually too, so a short, small overload does them no harm, and the breaker doesn’t trip at the first brief surge.

Short circuits trip the magnetic element. A short is a low-resistance path, such as a hot wire touching a neutral or ground, and the current can jump to hundreds of amps in an instant. The current flows through a small electromagnet in the breaker. At about 8 to 12 times the rating, the magnet yanks the latch open right away, with no waiting for anything to heat up.

Either way, the handle ends up at OFF or stuck partway between ON and OFF. To reset it, you push it fully off, then on (Being an Adult 101 shows how). A breaker that trips again right away is telling you there’s a fault.

blocks.html: Fuses and breakers are designed to protect conductors and equipment from overheating. A 15-amp breaker allows 15,000 milliamps, while OSHA lists 50 to 150 milliamps through the body as enough to stop breathing and possibly kill. Protecting people from shock is the job of the GFCI (Lesson 6).

Older homes may have fuses instead of breakers. A fuse contains a metal strip with a low melting point. Too much current heats it until it melts and opens the circuit for good, so it must be replaced, not reset.

The rule that matters most: replace a fuse only with one of the same rating. People sometimes swap a fuse that keeps blowing for a bigger one. That lets too much current flow and can overheat the wiring and start a fire. Never put anything other than a fuse in a fuse holder. CPSC suggests that, unless you are sure a circuit is a 20-amp circuit, a burned-out fuse be replaced with a 15-amp one, and that special non-interchangeable (Type S) fuse sockets be fitted so the wrong size won’t fit.

Panels and services are rated in amps. Berkeley Lab says the common sizes installed today are 100 and 200 amps, and older “legacy” sizes include 60 and 80 amps. In a 2026 Berkeley Lab study, 100-amp and 200-amp panels made up 55 and 29 percent of the panels in U.S. single-family homes. The University of Missouri Extension says homes heated with fuel need at least 100-amp service, and homes with electric heat need 150 to 200 amps.

Adding big loads, such as an electric-car charger or a heat pump, can push a home toward its limit. A full service upgrade is one answer. Others include load-management devices that switch off certain loads if a set limit is reached, which the 2023 edition of the National Electrical Code allows, sharing a circuit between two appliances, or choosing efficient appliances. An electrician does a load calculation to decide.

A subpanel is a smaller panel fed from the main panel by a heavy circuit called a feeder. It brings breakers closer to where the circuits are needed, such as a garage, a workshop or an addition. Adding one is a common alternative when the main panel is out of breaker spaces. Berkeley Lab found that at least 20 percent of panels of all sizes have no breaker space left.

blocks.h: Inside the panel is a licensed electrician’s job
blocks.html: Never take the cover off a panel. Behind it are live parts that can deliver a deadly shock or an arc. Switching off the main breaker doesn’t make everything inside safe: the wires from the utility connect to the main breaker itself, so they stay live. Replacing breakers, adding circuits and upgrading a service all need a licensed electrician, and usually a permit and inspection. If a panel is wet, scorched, buzzing or smells burned, don’t touch it: call an electrician, and if you see flashes or sparks at the service equipment, call the power company. If there’s smoke or fire, get everyone out and call 911.

• Reset a tripped breaker: push it fully off, then on. If it trips again right away, leave it off and call an electrician. Being an Adult 101 walks you through it.
  • Label your panel with a helper.
  • Replace a blown fuse with one of the same rating, and nothing bigger.
  • Keep a flashlight near the panel.

quiz.q: What does the thermal (bimetal) part of a breaker respond to?
opts: Overloads, with a delay that depends on how big the overload is
quiz.why: The bimetal strip heats with current squared multiplied by time, so a small overload trips slowly and a big one quickly.

quiz.q: Why does a dead short trip a breaker almost instantly?
opts: The huge current pulls the magnetic trip open
quiz.why: A short circuit can draw 8 to 12 times the rating or more, which trips the electromagnet at once.

quiz.q: Under UL 489, as CPSC describes it, a 20-amp breaker carrying 40 amps must trip within…
quiz.why: 40 amps is 200 percent of 20 amps, and the standard requires a trip within 2 minutes at 200 percent.

quiz.q: A fuse keeps blowing. What’s the right response?
opts: Find out why: the circuit is overloaded or has a fault
quiz.why: A bigger fuse lets the wires overheat. Unplug some loads, and if it still blows, call an electrician.

quiz.q: How many breaker spaces does a 240-volt circuit usually take?
opts: Two, one on each hot leg
quiz.why: A 240-volt circuit connects across both 120-volt legs, so it uses a double-width breaker.

lessons.title: Circuits and Wiring
lessons.short: Branch circuits wired in parallel, wire gauge and ampacity, cables and conduit, what the insulation colors mean, boxes, dedicated circuits, and why an overloaded circuit trips.
lessons.intro: From the panel, wires fan out to every room. Each run is a branch circuit, with its own breaker and its own limit. This lesson explains how those circuits are wired, what the wire sizes and colors mean, and why plugging in one more appliance can trip a breaker.

blocks.h: Branch circuits are wired in parallel
blocks.html:
A branch circuit is the wiring between the last breaker or fuse and the outlets it serves. A typical circuit feeds several outlets and lights. They’re wired in parallel: each one connects across the same hot and neutral wires, so each gets the full 120 volts, and turning one off doesn’t affect the others.

There’s a catch. In a parallel circuit, the currents add up. Every device draws its own current through its own branch, and all of it flows through the shared wire back to the breaker. The breaker sees the total.

Wire size in the U.S. is given as a gauge number (AWG). The smaller the number, the thicker the wire. Thicker wire has less resistance, so it heats less for the same current. A wire’s ampacity is the current it can carry continuously without getting too hot.

That’s why every circuit’s breaker is matched to its wire. The rule is that conductors must be protected from overcurrent according to their ability to carry current safely. Typical pairings for copper wire, from University of Missouri Extension, are in the table. The code and the conditions of each installation set the exact limits, so this is a guide to reading a circuit, not to designing one.

blocks.html:
Most homes use cable: insulated wires bundled in an outer jacket. Two-conductor cable has a black and a white wire; three-conductor cable adds a red one. Both usually include a bare or green-insulated ground wire too. In some buildings the wires run instead through a raceway such as metal or plastic conduit, an enclosed channel built to hold wires.

The insulation colors tell you each wire’s job:

  • Black or red (sometimes blue): hot, or “ungrounded,” wires that carry voltage.
  • White or gray: the neutral, or “grounded conductor,” that carries current back.
  • Green, green with yellow stripes, or bare: the equipment ground, which carries current only when something goes wrong.

Colors help, but they aren’t proof. Wiring can be old, altered or done wrong, and insulation colors vary by country. Never trust a color to tell you a wire is safe to touch: electricians test (Lesson 9).

Splices and connections are made inside boxes, such as junction boxes and the boxes behind outlets and switches, usually with twist-on wire connectors. Outlets and switches are called “devices”: parts that carry electricity but don’t use it.

Some appliances need a circuit of their own. Electric ranges, clothes dryers and water heaters get 240-volt circuits. Level 2 electric-car chargers usually need a dedicated circuit too; DOE’s Alternative Fuels Data Center says a typical 30-amp home charger requires a dedicated 40-amp circuit under the National Electrical Code. The U.S. Fire Administration says to plug major appliances such as refrigerators, stoves, washers and dryers directly into a wall outlet and never use an extension cord with them.

Add up the watts of everything running on one circuit and divide by 120 volts. If the total is more than the breaker’s rating, it will trip, quickly for a big overload and slowly for a small one (Lesson 3). For example, a 1,500-watt space heater plus a 1,000-watt microwave is 2,500 watts. Divided by 120 volts, that’s about 21 amps, too much for a 15-amp circuit and even a 20-amp one.

The fix is to move a load to a different circuit, not to fit a bigger breaker. Single plug-in loads have limits too. OSHA’s workplace rules cap one cord-and-plug load at 12 amps on a 15-amp receptacle and 16 amps on a 20-amp receptacle, 80 percent of the rating. Try it in the kitchen below.

blocks.html: Some homes built between 1965 and the mid-1970s were wired with aluminum branch-circuit wire. CPSC reports that homes built before 1972 and wired with aluminum were 55 times more likely to have one or more connections at outlets reach “fire hazard conditions” than homes wired with copper. The connections can overheat without warning. Signs CPSC lists include face plates on outlets or switches that are hot to the touch, flickering lights, circuits that don’t work, and the smell of burning plastic at outlets or switches. CPSC’s advice is to have a qualified electrician make one of its recommended repairs, and not to try it yourself.

lessons.title: Grounding and Bonding
lessons.short: What the ground wire is for, the fault-current path, grounding electrodes, bonding, polarized and three-prong plugs, and double insulation.
lessons.intro: Most of the time the ground wire does nothing at all. It’s there for the day something goes wrong, such as a frayed hot wire touching the metal case of a tool. This lesson explains how grounding and bonding turn that dangerous moment into a tripped breaker, and why your plugs are shaped the way they are.

blocks.html:
Modern wiring uses a three-wire system. The hot wire supplies voltage and current to the appliance. The neutral is the return path that completes the circuit. The third wire, the ground, connects to the metal case of the appliance. It carries no current in normal use.

The neutral is connected to the earth at the service, which holds it near zero volts. Even so, the neutral carries current whenever the circuit is on, and a loose connection or a wiring mistake can put voltage on it. Electricians treat every wire as live until they test it.

Picture a drill whose hot wire has rubbed through its insulation and is touching the metal housing. Now the housing is at 120 volts.

  • Without a ground wire, nothing happens until you pick up the drill while touching something grounded, like a faucet or damp floor. Then the current’s path to ground runs through you.
  • With the ground wire intact, the moment the hot wire touches the case, current rushes through the low-resistance ground wire back to the panel. That big current trips the breaker and shuts the power off. The tool stops working, which forces a repair.

OSHA puts it this way: a properly installed grounding conductor has a low resistance and greatly reduces the amount of current that passes through your body. Grounding is a backup protection, though. It doesn’t guarantee you won’t be shocked, which is one reason GFCIs exist (Lesson 6).

blocks.html: A breaker needs a lot of current to trip fast: at about 8 to 12 times its rating, the magnetic trip opens at once (Lesson 3). A solid, low-resistance ground path lets that big current flow, so the fault is cleared in a moment instead of leaving a live metal case. That’s why the path to ground must be permanent and continuous, and able to carry any fault current safely.

At the service, the neutral and the equipment ground wires are connected together, and both are connected to a grounding electrode through the grounding electrode conductor. A grounding electrode is a conductor buried in the earth. OSHA lists “made electrodes” such as metal rods, pipes and plates, and says a single rod, pipe or plate with more than 25 ohms of resistance to the earth must be backed up by a second electrode.

The earth connection ties the whole system to the ground around the house. It’s easy to think the earth is what trips the breaker, but the earth is a poor conductor compared with copper wire. Even a ground rod that just meets OSHA’s 25-ohm limit would pass only about 120 ÷ 25 ≈ 5 amps at 120 volts, not enough to trip a 15-amp breaker. When a metal case becomes live, the fault current returns mostly through the equipment ground wire to the panel, where the ground and neutral are tied together, and from there back toward the source. That low-resistance copper loop is what lets enough current flow to trip the breaker fast.

Bonding is the permanent joining of metal parts to form a continuous path that can carry any current likely to be put on it. A bonding jumper is a wire that connects metal parts that must be connected together. Metal boxes, conduit, panels and other metal parts that could become energized are bonded to the grounding system. If a hot wire touches any of them, the fault current has a path back and the breaker trips, instead of leaving a live piece of metal for someone to touch.

Plug shapes are part of the safety system:

  • Three-prong plugs have a grounding prong that connects the appliance’s metal case to the equipment ground. A standard three-prong plug fits only one way.
  • Polarized two-prong plugs have one blade wider than the other, so they fit an outlet only one way. That keeps the hot and neutral wires connected to the right parts of the appliance. The neutral should never be wired to the wrong terminal and reverse that polarity.
  • Double-insulated tools and appliances have two layers of insulation and no exposed metal parts, so they don’t need a ground prong. They’re marked as double-insulated.

Never force a three-prong plug into a two-slot outlet, and don’t bend the blades of a plug; bent blades usually cause worse overheating later. In older homes with two-slot outlets and no ground wire, a GFCI can still protect against shock. OSHA’s workplace rules allow a GFCI-protected replacement outlet where no ground exists if it’s marked “No Equipment Ground.” Adding that is a job for an electrician.

blocks.h: Leave grounding work to an electrician
blocks.html: Grounding and bonding are invisible when they work and dangerous when they don’t. Changing grounding connections, adding a ground wire, or replacing two-slot outlets is work for a licensed electrician. If you get even a slight shock or tingle from an appliance, a metal case or a faucet, don’t touch it again until an electrician has checked it.

quiz.q: What does the equipment ground wire carry during normal use?
quiz.why: The ground carries current only when something goes wrong. The neutral carries the normal return current.

quiz.q: A hot wire touches a grounded metal tool case. What should happen?
opts: A large current flows through the ground wire and trips the breaker
quiz.why: The low-resistance ground path lets a big fault current flow, which trips the breaker fast.

quiz.q: Why is one blade of a polarized plug wider?
opts: So it fits only one way and hot and neutral stay on the right sides
quiz.why: The asymmetric plug and outlet keep the hot and neutral connected to the right parts of the appliance.

quiz.q: According to OSHA, what happens if a single ground rod has more than 25 ohms of resistance to earth?
opts: It must be backed up by a second electrode
quiz.why: OSHA’s construction rule says a single rod, pipe or plate over 25 ohms must be augmented by one more electrode.

quiz.q: Why don’t double-insulated tools need a ground prong?
opts: Two layers of insulation and no exposed metal protect the user
quiz.why: Double insulation is an approved alternative to grounding, and such tools are marked to show it.

lessons.title: GFCIs, AFCIs and Other Protection
lessons.short: How a GFCI senses a current imbalance and how fast it trips, how an AFCI spots dangerous arcs, surge protection, tamper-resistant outlets, and smoke and CO alarms.
lessons.intro: A breaker protects the wires, but it can’t protect a person: the current that can kill you is far too small for a breaker to notice. Two smarter devices fill the gap. The GFCI guards against shock and the AFCI guards against fires from arcing. This lesson shows how each one works, along with the other safety devices in a modern home.

blocks.html:
A 15-amp breaker doesn’t trip until well over 15,000 milliamps flows. OSHA lists 50 to 150 milliamps through the body as enough to cause extreme pain and respiratory arrest, with death possible (Lesson 8). So a person can be badly hurt by a current the breaker will never notice.

A ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) closes that gap. OSHA defines it as a device for protecting people that shuts off a circuit when the current to ground goes over a set value that is less than what it takes to trip the breaker.

In a healthy circuit, every bit of current that goes out on the hot wire comes back on the neutral. A GFCI keeps checking that. Both wires pass through a small ring-shaped coil. When the two currents are equal and opposite, their magnetic fields cancel and the coil feels nothing. If some current leaks out another way, through a wet hand, a person or a faulty tool to ground, the two no longer match. The leftover field induces a voltage in the coil, and the GFCI’s circuit opens the contacts.

It reacts to tiny leaks. OSHA says a GFCI shuts off the power if the difference exceeds 5 milliamps, and can interrupt the current within as little as 1/40 of a second to prevent electrocution. NIOSH gives the trip level as 4 to 6 milliamps, and CPSC says as little as 6 milliamps. A GFCI also trips if the leak goes safely to ground through a ground wire, which forces you to find the problem.

A GFCI does not prevent you from feeling a shock. It doesn’t limit the current, and it can’t help if you touch the hot and neutral wires at the same time, because then the current out still equals the current back. What it does is cut the power fast, before a ground-fault shock lasts long enough to be deadly.

blocks.cap: Body resistance figures are NIOSH’s (dry skin 100,000 ohms or more, wet skin as low as 1,000 ohms); effects are from OSHA’s table. The trip level of 5 milliamps and time of 1/40 second are OSHA’s. The animation is slowed down so you can watch it.

blocks.h: Where GFCIs go and how to test them
blocks.html:
CPSC lists the places the National Electrical Code has required GFCI protection, added over the years starting in 1968: bathrooms, garages, kitchens, outdoor outlets, crawl spaces and unfinished basements, wet bar sinks, laundry and utility sinks, and underwater pool lighting. On construction sites, OSHA requires GFCI protection (or a special grounding program) for temporary 120-volt, 15- and 20-amp outlets.

There are three types. A GFCI breaker protects a whole circuit. A GFCI receptacle replaces an ordinary outlet and also protects the outlets wired after it. A portable GFCI plugs into an outlet, or is built into an extension cord, for temporary use such as outdoor tools.

Test each GFCI at least once a month, after a power failure, and as the maker directs: press TEST and the power should go off; press RESET and it should come back. Being an Adult 101 has the steps.

blocks.h: AFCIs: stopping fires before they start
blocks.html:
An arc is a glowing discharge of electricity across a gap. Problems in home wiring, such as loose connections, a cord crushed under furniture or wires damaged by age, can make arcs, and arcs can start fires. The U.S. Fire Administration found that electrical arcing was the heat source in 74 percent of the home electrical fires started by powered equipment in 2014 to 2016.

Ordinary breakers don’t respond to early arcing. CPSC staff explain why. A series arc, at a loose connection or a broken wire in a cord, is in line with the load, so the load limits its current to well below the breaker’s rating. A parallel arc, such as a hot wire arcing to a neutral or ground through damaged insulation, may flicker on and off too erratically to heat the breaker’s bimetal. By the time a breaker trips, a fire may already have started.

An arc-fault circuit interrupter (AFCI) uses electronics to tell normal arcing from the dangerous kind, which has an irregular pattern. When it sees a dangerous one, it shuts the circuit off. The 1999 National Electrical Code required AFCIs on bedroom circuits starting in 2002. Combination devices include both AFCI and GFCI protection in one unit. Like GFCIs, AFCIs have a test button and should be tested monthly. CPSC says to have a qualified electrician install AFCIs, and not to attempt the work yourself.

blocks.html:
A surge is a brief spike of voltage, from causes such as lightning or switching on the power system. NIST, which published a booklet for homeowners on the subject, calls surges unavoidable. Ready.gov recommends surge protection devices, and during a power outage it advises unplugging appliances and electronics to avoid damage from surges.

A power strip doesn’t add capacity to a circuit. The U.S. Fire Administration says not to overload power strips and to use ones with internal overload protection.

Tamper-resistant (TR) receptacles have built-in shutters behind the slots. The shutters open only when both blades of a plug push in together, so a child poking an object into one slot can’t reach the live metal. TR receptacles are required in some locations to protect children, and the U.S. Fire Administration recommends installing them if you have young children.

Smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) alarms are part of a home’s safety system too. The U.S. Fire Administration says to put smoke alarms inside and outside each bedroom and sleeping area, on the ceiling or high on the wall, and to test them monthly and replace them every 10 years. Interconnected alarms all sound when one does. Only qualified electricians should install hardwired smoke alarms, which usually have a backup battery to replace once a year. CPSC recommends CO alarms with battery backup outside sleeping areas and on each floor. When a smoke alarm sounds, you may have less than 2 minutes to get everyone out.

See Test Smoke and CO Alarms in Being an Adult 101 for how to test them and what to do when one goes off.

• Test every GFCI monthly: Test and Reset a GFCI Outlet.
  • Test AFCI breakers monthly with their TEST button, following the instructions on the device or panel.
  • Test smoke and CO alarms monthly: Test Smoke and CO Alarms.
  • Use a portable GFCI for outdoor power tools.

If a GFCI doesn’t cut the power when you press TEST, or RESET won’t bring the power back, don’t count on that outlet for protection: have a qualified electrician fix or replace it. Adding GFCI or AFCI protection, replacing a GFCI, and installing hardwired smoke alarms or whole-house surge protection are jobs for an electrician.

quiz.q: What does a GFCI compare?
opts: The current going out on the hot wire with the current coming back on the neutral
quiz.why: If some current is missing on the way back, it’s leaking another way, maybe through a person.

quiz.q: According to OSHA, at what difference does a GFCI shut off the power?
quiz.why: OSHA says a GFCI trips if the difference exceeds 5 milliamps, within as little as 1/40 of a second.

quiz.q: Why doesn’t an ordinary breaker catch a series arc at a loose connection?
opts: The arc current is limited by the load, so it stays below the breaker’s rating
quiz.why: A series arc is in line with the load, so its current is no bigger than the load’s normal current.

quiz.q: A GFCI’s light stays on when you press TEST. What does that mean?
opts: It isn’t protecting you; have a qualified electrician fix or replace it
quiz.why: A GFCI can keep delivering power after it stops protecting. That’s why you test monthly.

quiz.q: What do tamper-resistant outlets do?
opts: Use shutters so objects pushed into one slot can’t reach live parts
quiz.why: The shutters open only when both blades of a plug push in together.

lessons.title: Outlets, Switches and Lights
lessons.short: Receptacle types and ratings, how single-pole, 3-way and 4-way switches work, dimmers, and LED lighting and its efficiency.
lessons.intro: Outlets, switches and lights are the parts of the electrical system you touch every day. This lesson explains what the slots and screws on an outlet mean, how two switches at opposite ends of a hallway can both control one light, and why LED bulbs use so little power.

blocks.html:
The everyday outlet is properly called a receptacle: a contact device at an outlet where you connect a plug. The most common kind in homes is a duplex (two-outlet) receptacle rated for 15 amps at 125 volts. The narrow slot connects to the hot wire, the wider slot to the neutral, and the third hole to the equipment ground. Inside the wall, the black hot wire goes to the brass-colored screw, the white neutral to the silver screw, and the bare or green ground to the green screw.

Ratings have to match the circuit. OSHA’s workplace rules allow only 15-amp receptacles on a 15-amp circuit; a 20-amp circuit can have 15- or 20-amp receptacles. Receptacles for different voltages, such as 240-volt dryer and range outlets, are shaped so the wrong plug won’t fit.

When a plug wobbles or falls out of an outlet easily, the contacts inside are worn. Loose-fitting plugs can overheat and cause fires, so CPSC says to have the outlet replaced.

blocks.html: A single-pole switch is the simplest: two terminal screws and an ON/OFF lever. Flip it on and it closes a gap in the circuit so current can flow to the light; flip it off and it opens the gap. Many switches also have a green screw for the ground wire.

A hallway or stairway light usually has a switch at each end. Either switch can turn the light on or off, no matter where the other one is. That takes a pair of 3-way switches; they always come in pairs.

A 3-way switch has no ON or OFF. It has one common terminal (usually a darker screw) and two traveler terminals, and its lever connects the common to one traveler or the other. At one switch the common is connected to the power source; at the other, the common goes to the light. Two traveler wires run between the switches, usually in a three-conductor cable with black, red and white wires plus a ground.

Current reaches the light only when both switches are set to the same traveler. Flip either one and the path breaks. Flip either one again and it’s complete. To control a light from three or more places, electricians add 4-way switches between the two 3-ways. A 4-way swaps the two travelers: in one position they pass straight through, in the other they cross over. Try it below.

blocks.cap: Wire colors follow the cable described by Purdue Extension 4-H. Real installations vary, and in some the power feeds the light first. The current path, not the color, is what matters.

blocks.html: A dimmer lets you set the brightness of a light. The U.S. Department of Energy says most LEDs are dimmable, and dimmer-compatible LEDs are widely available. Not every LED works with every dimmer, though, so check the bulb’s package and the dimmer’s instructions to be sure they work together.

An old incandescent bulb makes light by heating a wire filament until it glows. About 90 percent of its energy comes out as heat and only about 10 percent as light. LEDs make light directly from electronics. DOE says LEDs use up to 90 percent less energy and last up to 25 times longer than incandescent bulbs, and stay cool to the touch.

Shop for lumens, a measure of brightness, not watts. DOE says that to replace a 75-watt incandescent bulb, look for an LED of about 1,100 lumens; a screw-in LED can do it with as little as 9 watts. The Lighting Facts label shows brightness, yearly energy cost, expected life and light color. Color is given in kelvins (K): lower numbers look warmer and more yellow, higher numbers cooler and bluer.

Every fixture has a maximum bulb wattage on its label. A bulb with more watts than the fixture allows can overheat the fixture and its wiring. LEDs make it easy to stay under the limit.

blocks.html:
Whether you may replace your own switch or receptacle depends on where you live: some places allow homeowners to do it, often with a permit, and others require a licensed electrician. Either way, these are the principles electricians follow:

  • Always de-energize the circuit first, at the breaker.
  • Prove it’s dead with a voltage tester rated for the job, after checking the tester on a known live source, and check it again afterward (Lesson 9).
  • Replace like with like: the same amp rating, and GFCI or tamper-resistant protection where it’s required.
  • Stop if you find aluminum wiring, scorched or brittle insulation, or anything you don’t understand, and call an electrician.

• Replace bulbs with LEDs that don’t exceed the fixture’s wattage limit.
  • Choose LEDs labeled as dimmable for lights on dimmers.
  • Notice loose-fitting plugs and warm switch plates, and have them checked.
  • Test GFCI receptacles monthly: Being an Adult 101.

quiz.q: On a standard receptacle, which slot connects to the neutral?
quiz.why: The wider slot is the neutral, the narrow one is hot, and the third hole is the ground.

quiz.q: Two 3-way switches control one light. When is the light on?
opts: When both switches connect their commons to the same traveler
Only when one switch is off
quiz.why: There’s a complete path only when both switches select the same traveler wire.

quiz.q: What do you add to control a light from a third place?
quiz.why: A 4-way switch either passes the travelers straight through or crosses them.

quiz.q: What should you look for to replace a 75-watt incandescent bulb?
quiz.why: Brightness is measured in lumens. DOE says about 1,100 lumens, which an LED can give with as little as 9 watts.

quiz.q: What can a 20-amp circuit have, under OSHA’s receptacle rules?
quiz.why: A 15-amp circuit may have only 15-amp receptacles; a 20-amp circuit may have 15- or 20-amp ones.

lessons.short: What current does to the body, why water makes it worse, why electricians never work live, lockout/tagout, overhead power lines, extension cords and power strips, and electrical fires.
lessons.intro: Electricity is invisible, silent and fast. That’s what makes it dangerous. This lesson uses figures from OSHA, NIOSH, CPSC and the U.S. Fire Administration to show what current does to the body, why wet skin changes everything, and the habits that keep electricians alive.

blocks.html: A shock happens when your body becomes part of a circuit. How bad it is depends on how much current flows through you, the path it takes, how long it lasts, and its frequency. The body is most sensitive to the 50- and 60-hertz frequencies used for power. OSHA’s table, for current flowing from hand to foot for one second, shows how little it takes:

blocks.html:
Ohm’s law says current equals voltage divided by resistance. Most of your body’s resistance is in your skin, and water changes it enormously. NIOSH says dry skin may have a resistance of 100,000 ohms or more, but wet skin may have only 1,000 ohms. At 120 volts:

  • Dry skin: 120 ÷ 100,000 = 1.2 milliamps. A faint tingle.
  • Wet skin: 120 ÷ 1,000 = 120 milliamps. In OSHA’s 50-to-150 milliamp range, where breathing can stop and death is possible.

The OpenStax textbook uses different estimates, 200,000 ohms dry and 10,000 ohms soaking wet, and reaches the same lesson: getting wet can raise the current by a factor of ten or more, past the point where you can let go. OSHA adds that pure water is a poor conductor, but the small amounts of salt and other impurities in real water make it conduct, and wet skin acts as a conductor. That’s why outlets near sinks, tubs and outdoors need GFCIs (Lesson 6).
I = V ÷ R  <small>(120 V ÷ 1,000 Ω = 0.12 A = 120 mA)</small>

Electricians plan their work so they never touch anything energized. OSHA’s rules say parts that have been switched off but not locked out or tagged must be treated as if they’re still energized, and only qualified people may work on energized parts. NIOSH puts it simply: always test a circuit to make sure it is de-energized before working on it.

On the job, that means lockout/tagout. OSHA says the first step before any inspection or repair is to turn the current off at the switch box and padlock the switch in the OFF position, so no one can switch it back on by mistake, and a tag warns others. Then a qualified person tests to prove the parts are dead (Lesson 9).

Overhead power lines are usually not insulated. OSHA tells workers to stay at least 10 feet away from overhead power lines and to assume they are energized. Its rule for workers who aren’t qualified for power-line work sets a 10-foot clearance for lines up to 50,000 volts, plus 4 inches for every 10,000 volts above that, and the same for ladders, poles and equipment they’re holding or using. Ladders used near live parts must have nonconductive side rails.

Never go near a downed or fallen power line. It can electrocute you if you touch it or the ground nearby, and it can energize fences and other objects it touches. Call the utility. If a power line falls on your car, OSHA says to stay inside unless the vehicle is on fire.

blocks.html:
CPSC has estimated that about 2,000 home fires a year are associated with electric cords or plugs, killing 60 people. Its advice and the U.S. Fire Administration’s:

  • Use extension cords only when necessary and only temporarily. They aren’t as safe as permanent wiring.
  • Don’t overload a cord or power strip. Use power strips with internal overload protection.
  • Never use an extension cord with a major appliance; plug those straight into the wall.
  • Use three-wire cords for appliances with three-prong plugs, and cords labeled for outdoor use outdoors.
  • Don’t run cords under rugs or furniture, and don’t nail or staple them in place.
  • Replace cracked, worn or damaged cords. Don’t repair them.

Cord size matters as much as wire size in the walls. CPSC warns that thin 18-gauge cords will overheat if they carry 15 amps.

In 2021, U.S. fire departments responded to an estimated 24,200 home electrical fires, which caused about 295 deaths, 900 injuries and over $1.2 billion in property loss, according to the U.S. Fire Administration. In its study of 2014 to 2016, electrical fires most often started in bedrooms and in attics or crawl spaces, and wiring and outlets were the most common equipment involved.

Warning signs CPSC lists include breakers or fuses that trip often, lights that dim or flicker, sparks, sizzling or buzzing sounds, switch plates or cords that are hot or discolored, a smell of hot insulation, and any shock, even a mild tingle. Stop using that outlet, switch or appliance and have an electrician check it.

If there’s fire or smoke, get everyone out and call 911 from outside, on a mobile phone or from a neighbor’s. Fire extinguishers rated Class C are made for fires in plugged-in electrical equipment, because their agent doesn’t conduct electricity. The U.S. Fire Administration says to use an extinguisher only if the fire is small and contained, you’re safe from the smoke, and you have a clear way out; otherwise, leave.

• Treat every wire as live until a qualified person has tested it and proven it dead.
  • Keep electrical devices and cords away from water, and never touch them with wet hands or while standing in water.
  • Stay at least 10 feet from overhead lines, and far away from downed ones.
  • Any shock or tingle from an appliance, switch or faucet means stop using it until an electrician has checked it.

quiz.q: According to OSHA, about what current can cause respiratory arrest, with death possible?
quiz.why: OSHA lists 50 to 150 milliamps as causing extreme pain, respiratory arrest and severe muscle contractions.

quiz.q: With NIOSH’s wet-skin figure of 1,000 ohms, how much current would 120 volts drive?
What does lockout/tagout prevent?
opts: Someone switching the power back on while you work
quiz.why: A padlock and tag on the switch keep it OFF until the person who placed them removes them.

quiz.q: How far does OSHA tell workers to stay from overhead power lines?
quiz.why: Stay at least 10 feet away and assume the lines are energized; more for higher voltages.

quiz.q: A cord feels hot when a heater is plugged into it. What’s the best move?
opts: Unplug and use a properly rated cord, or plug the heater straight into the wall
quiz.why: A hot cord is overloaded or too small. Heaters and major appliances belong in a wall outlet.

lessons.title: Testing Tools and “Test Before Touch”
lessons.short: Non-contact voltage testers and their limits, multimeters, plug-in testers, how electricians verify a circuit is dead, and what homeowners can safely test.
lessons.intro: Electricians have a rule: you don’t know a wire is dead until you’ve tested it, and you don’t trust the test until you’ve tested the tester. This lesson explains the tools of the trade, what each can and can’t tell you, and the simple tests anyone can do at home.

blocks.html: Switching off a breaker should make a circuit dead. But a panel label can be wrong, a box can hold wires from more than one circuit, and old wiring may not be what it seems. OSHA’s advice is to treat everything electrical as energized until it has been tested and proven to be de-energized. NIOSH says the same: always test a circuit before working on it.

A non-contact voltage tester is a pen-shaped tool that beeps or lights up when it’s near an energized AC wire. It senses the electric field around the wire without touching metal, which makes it handy for a quick check, such as finding which cable is live.

It has real limits. The U.S. Department of Energy’s electrical safety handbook says these “proximity testers” must not be used to test for the absence of voltage, because a tester’s failure to detect voltage doesn’t guarantee the equipment is de-energized. They don’t detect DC, or AC inside a shielded cable, and a fault or a weak battery can silence them. In 2021, CPSC announced a recall of one brand’s testers because a sticking button could keep them from warning users of live voltage. Virginia Tech’s safety office allows them only as a secondary check.

A digital multimeter measures voltage, resistance and sometimes current. To prove there’s no voltage, electricians touch the meter’s probes to the conductors. DOE says the absence of voltage should be verified only with a voltmeter rated for the job. Meters carry a category (CAT) rating that tells which kinds of circuits they’re built to withstand, and DOE calls for category-rated, listed meters.

A tester that reads “nothing” might be telling the truth, or it might be broken. So electricians use a three-step routine, sometimes called live–dead–live:

  1. Live: test a known energized source to prove the tester works.
  2. Dead: test the circuit you’ll work on and confirm there’s no voltage.
  3. Live: test the known source again to prove the tester still works.

Only if the tester still works and showed no voltage can the equipment be considered de-energized. For equipment over 600 volts, OSHA requires checking the test equipment immediately before and after the test.

blocks.html: A plug-in receptacle tester has lights that show whether an outlet has power and point to some common wiring mistakes; the meaning of each light pattern is printed on the tester. A small lamp or night-light you know works is the simplest tester of all, and it’s what Being an Adult 101 uses to test GFCIs. Both are good for answering “does this outlet have power?” Neither proves that wires are safe to touch.

Plenty of testing needs no tools and opens no covers:

  • Press TEST on every GFCI once a month, then RESET (Being an Adult 101).
  • Press TEST on AFCI breakers monthly, as CPSC recommends.
  • Test smoke and CO alarms monthly (Being an Adult 101).
  • Reset a tripped breaker and find which outlets it controls with a lamp (Being an Adult 101).
  • Check that outlets and switch plates are cool to the touch and that plugs fit snugly.

Measuring voltage inside panels, boxes or equipment is different. It means working near live parts, which OSHA and university safety programs limit to qualified people.

blocks.h: Testing is not a license to work live
blocks.html: A tester is a tool for proving something is dead before work begins, not a way to make live work safe. Opening panels and measuring live circuits is a job for qualified electricians with the right meters and protective equipment. If any test surprises you, such as power where you didn’t expect it, stop and call an electrician.

quiz.q: Why can’t a non-contact tester prove a wire is dead?
opts: It may miss voltage, for example in a shielded cable or with a weak battery
quiz.why: DOE says proximity testers must not be used to test for the absence of voltage.

quiz.q: What is the “live–dead–live” routine?
opts: Checking the tester on a known live source before and after testing the circuit
Turning a breaker on, off and on
quiz.why: If the tester works before and after, a “dead” reading on the circuit can be trusted.

quiz.q: What does DOE say should be used to verify the absence of voltage?
opts: A voltmeter rated for the application
quiz.why: A rated voltmeter, with its operation checked on a known source.

quiz.q: Which test can any homeowner do safely each month?
opts: Press TEST and RESET on GFCIs
quiz.why: GFCI and AFCI test buttons and smoke and CO alarms are made for regular testing by anyone.

lessons.title: EV Charging, Solar, Batteries and Generators
lessons.short: Level 1 and Level 2 electric-car charging, rooftop solar and inverters, home batteries, and portable and standby generators, with carbon monoxide and backfeeding dangers.
lessons.intro: Homes don’t only use electricity anymore. Many charge cars, make their own power from sunlight, store it in batteries, or keep a generator for outages. Each of these connects to the same panel and wiring you’ve been learning about, and each brings its own safety rules.

blocks.html:
DOE’s Alternative Fuels Data Center describes three levels of charging:

  • Level 1 uses a 120-volt AC plug and adds about 5 miles of range per hour of charging, at about 1.9 kilowatts. Many drivers meet their daily needs by charging overnight this way, on an outlet on a dedicated branch circuit near where they park.
  • Level 2 uses 240 volts at home (208 volts is typical in commercial buildings) and adds about 25 miles of range per hour. Most home Level 2 chargers run at up to 30 amps, delivering 7.2 kilowatts (30 × 240 = 7,200 watts), and need a dedicated 40-amp circuit under the National Electrical Code.
  • DC fast charging adds about 100 to 200 or more miles in 30 minutes, at up to 500 kilowatts. It needs heavy commercial power, so it’s found along highways, not in homes.

Installing Level 2 at home is a job for a qualified electrician. Some homes don’t have enough electrical capacity, permits may be required, and in many areas a plan must be approved before installation. Charging equipment that’s certified for safety is recommended, and outdoor installations need outdoor-rated equipment. The Cars course explains the car side.

Solar panels are made of photovoltaic (PV) cells that turn sunlight directly into electricity. A single cell makes only about 1 or 2 watts, so cells are wired together into weather-tight panels, and panels into arrays. The best modules today approach 25 percent efficiency, up from under 10 percent in the mid-1980s.

PV cells make direct current, but your home and the grid run on alternating current. Inverters convert the DC to AC. Since 2004, most U.S. PV systems have been grid-connected, wired into the home’s panel and the utility’s lines. Small grid-connected systems, mostly on homes and buildings, made about 93 billion kWh in 2025.

A battery lets a solar system supply electricity when the sun isn’t shining. EIA counts batteries under 1 megawatt as “small-scale,” and many are owned by people who charge them from their own solar panels. In 2021, U.S. utilities in 42 states reported about 1,094 megawatts of small-scale battery capacity. Whether a solar-and-battery system can power a home during a grid outage depends on how it’s designed and installed, so ask the installer.

blocks.html:
A portable generator is an engine, and its exhaust contains carbon monoxide (CO), a gas you can’t see or smell. CPSC says more than 80 consumers die each year from CO poisoning caused by portable generators. The official rules:

  • Use a generator only outside, at least 20 feet from the house, with the exhaust pointed away from the home and other buildings (CPSC, Ready.gov).
  • Never run it inside a home, garage, basement, crawlspace or shed, even with doors and windows open (CPSC).
  • Install battery-operated CO alarms, or plug-in alarms with battery backup, outside sleeping areas and on each floor (CPSC). If a CO alarm sounds, get outside immediately, then call 911.
  • Keep the generator dry, and plug appliances into it with heavy-duty, outdoor-rated, grounded cords rated for the load (OSHA, CPSC).

Never try to power a house by plugging a generator into a wall outlet. CPSC and OSHA both warn against it. Connecting a generator to a building’s wiring without a properly installed transfer switch can send power back out through the wiring, a hazard called backfeeding. OSHA warns that it can energize wiring for great distances, creating a risk of electrocution for utility workers and others in the area.

The safe way to connect a generator to a home’s circuits is a transfer switch, which disconnects the house from the utility before connecting the generator. OSHA says never to attach a generator to a structure’s electrical system unless a qualified electrician has installed it with a transfer switch.

A standby, or stationary, generator is installed permanently outside and connected to the home through a transfer switch, often an automatic one that starts the generator when the power fails. CPSC staff say these are typically installed by licensed tradespeople following the National Electrical Code and the maker’s instructions, and must meet local codes. They still make CO. In a June 2025 report, CPSC staff found exhaust traveling at least 25 feet from generator enclosures and concluded that the 5-foot clearance from openings allowed by the NFPA 37 standard is not enough to keep CO out of homes.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting by Symptom
lessons.short: An interactive finder: pick a symptom, answer one question, and get the likely causes, what you can safely check, and when to stop and call an electrician.
lessons.intro: When something electrical goes wrong, the first question isn’t “how do I fix it?” but “is this dangerous right now?” This lesson gives you a way to think it through and a finder that turns common symptoms into likely causes, safe checks and a clear point to stop.

blocks.html:
Before anything else, ask:

  1. Is anything hot, smoking, sparking, buzzing or smelling burned? Those are CPSC’s warning signs of a wiring problem. Stop using that outlet, switch or appliance. If there’s smoke or fire, get everyone out and call 911.
  2. Did anyone feel a shock or a tingle? CPSC says any shock, even a mild tingle, may be a warning. Don’t touch that appliance or fixture again until an electrician has checked it.
  3. How big is the problem? One outlet, one circuit, the whole house, or the whole street? The answer points to a GFCI, a breaker, your service or the utility.

blocks.h: How an electrician thinks it through
blocks.html:
Electricians work from the source toward the problem. Is there power at the meter and the main panel? Is the breaker for that circuit on? Is a GFCI upstream tripped? Is power reaching the box, and are the connections there sound? Each “yes” narrows the search. Most of those checks mean opening boxes and testing live circuits, which is why they’re a qualified electrician’s job. Your part is the first few questions and a good description: what happened, when, what was running, and what you smelled or heard.

Keep notes. CPSC lists breakers that trip often, lights that dim or flicker, and hot outlets as signs worth reporting, and a pattern (“it trips every morning when the space heater and the coffee maker run”) helps an electrician find the cause faster.

blocks.html: Heat, smoke, sparks, buzzing from a panel, a burning smell, a shock, or a downed power line all mean stop. Don’t reset, don’t investigate and don’t touch. Get people clear, call 911 for fire or smoke, call the utility for lines and service problems, and call an electrician for everything else.

quiz.q: A kitchen outlet is dead but the breaker is on. What’s the first safe check?
opts: Look for a tripped GFCI nearby and press RESET
Use an extension cord from another room
quiz.why: A GFCI protects the outlets wired after it, and it may be in another room.

quiz.q: You smell burning plastic near an outlet. What should you do?
opts: Stop using it; if there’s smoke or fire, get out and call 911; have an electrician check it
quiz.why: A burning smell is one of CPSC’s warning signs of overheated wiring.

quiz.q: Your whole house is dark and so is the neighbors’. Who do you call?
quiz.why: A neighborhood outage is the utility’s to fix.

quiz.q: A breaker trips again right after you reset it. What does that suggest?
opts: A fault such as a short circuit; leave it off and call an electrician
quiz.why: An immediate trip points to a fault, not an overload.

lessons.title: Doing Your Own Work
lessons.short: Permits, inspections and licensing rules that vary by place, a basic tool kit, safety principles, and the skill ladder from resetting breakers to jobs for a licensed electrician.
lessons.intro: Electrical work is the one home trade where a small mistake can hide inside a wall for years and then start a fire, or hurt someone right away. That’s why it’s the most regulated. This lesson explains who is allowed to do what, the tools worth owning, and a ladder of skills from your first safe jobs to the ones that belong with a licensed electrician.

blocks.html:
The rules are set by states, counties and cities, and they vary a lot. Most states require electricians to pass a test and be licensed, and their tests cover the National Electrical Code and state and local codes. Building and electrical regulations in most places are based on the National Electrical Code (NFPA 70), a model code that each state or city adopts, sometimes with changes of its own.

Some places let homeowners do certain electrical work on the home they own and live in, usually with a permit and an inspection. Others require a licensed electrician for almost everything. Even simple jobs may need a permit; for example, DOE notes that installing an electric-car charger may need permits from the local building authority, and in many areas a plan approved before the work starts. Before any electrical project, ask your local building or permit office what the rules are where you live.

Permits and inspections protect you. An inspector checks work before it’s hidden in the walls.

blocks.html:
For the jobs on the first rungs of the ladder, you need very little:

  • A flashlight kept near the panel.
  • A small lamp or night-light you know works, for checking outlets and GFCIs.
  • Labels and a pen for the panel directory.
  • A plug-in GFCI for outdoor tools and wet areas.
  • A multimeter with a category (CAT) rating suited to household circuits, and a non-contact voltage tester as a secondary check, if you go on to learn testing. Neither is a license to work near live parts (Lesson 9).

These are the habits electricians live by. They aren’t step-by-step instructions for any job:

  • Power off at the source. De-energize the circuit at the breaker before touching any device or wire, and make sure no one can switch it back on.
  • Test before you touch. Prove the circuit is dead with a rated tester checked on a known live source before and after (Lesson 9).
  • Match the ratings. Breakers match the wire, receptacles match the circuit, and bulbs stay under the fixture’s limit.
  • Keep the protection. GFCI, AFCI and tamper-resistant protection stay where they’re required.
  • Stop when you’re unsure. Aluminum wiring, scorch marks, brittle insulation, or anything you don’t recognize means call an electrician.

lessons.title: Careers in Electrical Work
lessons.short: What electricians do, how they train through apprenticeships, licensing and the National Electrical Code, what they earn, and the job outlook.
lessons.intro: Electricians wire new homes and repair old ones, keep factories running, and install the chargers, solar panels and batteries that are changing how buildings use power. It’s a skilled trade you can learn while being paid. Here’s what the work involves and how people get into it, with the latest figures from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

blocks.html:
Electricians install, maintain and repair electrical power, communications, lighting and control systems. On a typical day they might:

  • Read blueprints or technical diagrams.
  • Install and maintain wiring, control and lighting systems.
  • Inspect electrical components such as transformers and circuit breakers.
  • Find electrical problems using a variety of testing devices.
  • Repair or replace wiring, equipment or fixtures with hand and power tools.
  • Follow state and local building regulations based on the National Electrical Code.
  • Direct and train workers.

The work can be physically demanding, and it has real hazards: BLS says common injuries include electrical shocks, falls and burns. That’s why safety training is part of every apprenticeship.
Here are the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics figures from the Occupational Outlook Handbook (page last modified August 27, 2026):

In May 2025, the lowest-paid 10 percent of electricians earned less than $42,640 a year and the highest-paid 10 percent more than $108,510. Median pay varied by industry: $79,820 in government, $74,550 in manufacturing, $61,570 for electrical contractors and other wiring installation contractors, and $57,760 in employment services. Projected growth of 9 percent from 2025 to 2035 is much faster than average, and about 72,700 openings are expected each year.

Most electricians learn the trade in a 4- or 5-year apprenticeship. For each year of the program, apprentices typically receive 2,000 hours of paid on-the-job training plus technical instruction in electrical theory, blueprint reading, mathematics, electrical code requirements, and safety and first-aid practices. Several groups, including unions and contractor associations, sponsor apprenticeship programs. Many technical schools offer programs in circuitry, safety practices and basic electrical information, and workers with electrical experience in the military or construction may qualify for a shortened apprenticeship. After finishing, electricians are considered journey workers, and they may later advance to master electrician.

Apprenticeship.gov describes a registered apprenticeship as an industry-driven, high-quality career pathway. Apprentices get paid work experience with a mentor, progressive wage increases, classroom instruction, and a portable, nationally recognized credential. You can search for openings with the Apprenticeship Job Finder at Apprenticeship.gov.

blocks.h: Licensing and the National Electrical Code
blocks.html:
Most states require electricians to pass a test and be licensed. The tests have questions on the National Electrical Code and on state and local electrical codes. Electricians may also need continuing education to keep their licenses.

The National Electrical Code, also called NFPA 70, is written by the National Fire Protection Association and published in new editions every few years; the 2023 edition, for example, allows load-management systems that can avoid some panel upgrades. It’s a model code: it becomes law only when a state or city adopts it, sometimes with local changes. That’s why “what the code says” always means the code your local inspector enforces.

• Take algebra, physics and any shop or technical classes your school offers.
  • Learn the basics in this course and in Being an Adult 101.
  • Play with circuits in the Circuit Builder.
  • Look up registered apprenticeships near you on Apprenticeship.gov, and check your state’s licensing board for its rules.
