opts.label: Right away when you reset it, even with everything unplugged
causes: A short circuit or ground fault in the wiring or in something still connected
A damaged outlet, switch or fixture on that circuit
A failing breaker
checks: Leave the breaker off.
Note which outlets and lights are dead and what was running when it tripped.
opts.stop: Don’t keep resetting it. A breaker that trips again right away is protecting you from a fault.
opts.pro: Call a licensed electrician to find the fault.

opts.label: When certain appliances run at the same time
causes: An overload: the appliances together draw more amps than the breaker allows
High-wattage heaters, kettles, hair dryers or toasters sharing one circuit
checks: Add up the watts on that circuit and divide by 120 to get amps.
Move one appliance to a different circuit.
Reset the breaker: push it fully off, then on.
opts.stop: Never replace the breaker with a bigger one; the wire would overheat first.
opts.pro: If it still trips with a light load, or you need more circuits, call an electrician.

opts.label: It’s an AFCI or GFCI breaker, and it trips now and then
causes: A plugged-in appliance or cord with a fault
Moisture in an outdoor or garage outlet (GFCI)
Damaged wiring or a loose connection (AFCI)
checks: Unplug everything on the circuit, reset, then plug things back in one at a time to see which one trips it.
Look for damaged cords and stop using any that are.
opts.stop: If a particular appliance trips it, stop using that appliance.
opts.pro: If it trips with nothing plugged in, have an electrician check the circuit.

opts.label: Just one or a few outlets, near a kitchen, bath, garage or outdoors
causes: A tripped GFCI, which may be on another outlet, even in another room
A tripped GFCI breaker in the panel
checks: Look for GFCI outlets nearby (kitchen, bathrooms, garage, basement, outside) and press RESET.
Check the panel for a tripped breaker.
Test the outlet with a lamp you know works.
opts.stop: If the GFCI trips again at once, unplug what was running and check its cord.
opts.pro: If RESET won’t restore power, have a qualified electrician check it.

opts.label: A whole room or area is dark
causes: A tripped breaker
A blown fuse in an older home
checks: Turn off and unplug things in the dark area.
Find the tripped breaker and reset it, or replace the fuse with one of the same rating.
opts.stop: If it trips again right away, leave it off.
opts.pro: Call an electrician if it keeps tripping or you can’t find the cause.

opts.label: The outlet is warm, discolored or smells burned
causes: An overheated connection or a failing receptacle
Aluminum branch wiring in some homes built from 1965 to the mid-1970s
checks: Stop using the outlet and unplug what you safely can.
Turn off its breaker if you can do so safely.
opts.stop: If there’s smoke or fire, get everyone out and call 911.
opts.pro: Have an electrician check it before you use it again.

finder.name: GFCI won’t reset or keeps tripping

opts.label: It trips when one particular appliance is plugged in
causes: A fault in that appliance or its cord leaking current to ground
checks: Unplug the appliance and reset the GFCI.
Look for a damaged cord.
opts.stop: Stop using the appliance; the GFCI is doing its job.
opts.pro: Have the appliance repaired or replaced.

opts.label: It trips with nothing plugged in, or after rain
causes: Moisture in an outdoor or garage outlet or its box
A fault in the wiring after the GFCI
A worn-out GFCI
checks: Make sure outdoor outlet covers are closed.
Let things dry, then try RESET.
opts.stop: Don’t keep resetting a GFCI that trips with nothing connected.
opts.pro: Have a qualified electrician find the leak.

opts.label: RESET won’t work at all, or TEST doesn’t cut the power
causes: The circuit’s breaker is off, so the GFCI has no power
The GFCI has failed
checks: Check the panel for a tripped breaker.
Test with a lamp you know works.
opts.stop: If TEST doesn’t cut the power, that outlet isn’t protecting anyone.
opts.pro: Have a qualified electrician replace it.

opts.label: One lamp or fixture
causes: A loose or failing bulb
An LED that isn’t made for the dimmer it’s on
A worn lamp switch or cord
checks: With the light off, check that the bulb is screwed in.
Try a new bulb; on a dimmer, use one labeled dimmable.
Check the lamp cord for damage.
opts.stop: If the fixture or switch plate is warm or crackles, stop using it.
opts.pro: If a new bulb doesn’t fix a fixture, have an electrician check it.

opts.label: Many lights, often, or some get brighter as others dim
causes: A loose connection in the panel or the service
A problem with the utility’s service wires
Aluminum wiring connections overheating
checks: Note when it happens and what’s running.
Look (from a distance) for damaged or sagging service wires outside.
opts.stop: Don’t touch the panel or service equipment. If you see sparks there, call the utility.
opts.pro: Call the utility and an electrician right away.

finder.name: Lights dim when a big appliance starts

opts.label: A brief dip as it starts, then back to normal
causes: Motors draw extra current as they start
A circuit or service near its limit
checks: Notice whether it’s getting worse.
Move other loads off the circuit that dims.
opts.stop: Stop using a circuit if anything gets warm or smells.
opts.pro: Have an electrician check that the circuit and service are adequate, as University of Missouri Extension advises for dimming.

opts.label: A deep dim, flickering, or it’s getting worse
causes: A loose or failing connection
An overloaded or undersized service
checks: Turn off the appliance if you can do so safely.
Note what’s running.
opts.stop: Don’t touch the panel. If there are sparks, smoke or a burning smell, get out and call 911.
opts.pro: Call an electrician soon, and the utility if many lights are affected.

opts.label: An outlet or switch plate is warm or discolored
causes: A loose or overheated connection
An overloaded outlet
A worn receptacle with loose contacts
Aluminum wiring connections
checks: Stop using it and unplug what you safely can.
Turn off its breaker if you can do so safely.
opts.stop: CPSC says outlets and switches should never be hot to the touch: stop using them until an electrician checks.
opts.pro: Call an electrician.

opts.label: A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke or sparks
causes: Overheated wiring or a failing device
An appliance or cord overheating
checks: If there’s smoke or fire, get everyone out and call 911 from outside.
If it’s a plug-in appliance and you can safely unplug it, do.
opts.stop: Don’t stay to investigate a fire. Use an extinguisher only if the fire is small and contained and you have a clear way out.
opts.pro: Have an electrician check before you use the circuit again.

opts.label: A cord or plug feels hot
causes: An overloaded or undersized extension cord
A loose-fitting plug in a worn outlet
checks: Unplug it.
Plug heaters and major appliances directly into the wall.
Replace damaged cords; don’t repair them.
opts.stop: Never run cords under rugs or use extension cords as permanent wiring.
opts.pro: If plugs fit loosely in an outlet, have the outlet replaced.

opts.label: From an outlet, switch or fixture
causes: Arcing at a loose connection
A failing device
checks: Stop using it.
Turn off its breaker if you can do so safely.
opts.stop: CPSC lists sizzling or buzzing as a warning sign of a wiring problem.
opts.pro: Call an electrician.

opts.label: From the panel or the meter
causes: A loose or arcing connection in the panel or service equipment
checks: Stay away from it.
opts.stop: Don’t touch the panel or service equipment. If you see flashes or sparks, call the utility.
opts.pro: Call an electrician or the utility right away.

finder.name: Part of the house lost power

opts.label: Some rooms, or only 240-volt appliances like the dryer or range
causes: A tripped breaker, including a two-pole 240-volt one
A problem with one of the two incoming 120-volt legs of the service
checks: Check the panel for tripped breakers and reset one that’s tripped.
See whether neighbors have similar trouble.
opts.stop: If lights look unusually bright or dim, unplug sensitive electronics.
opts.pro: If no breaker is tripped, call the utility first, then an electrician.

opts.label: One area after a storm, with wires down outside
causes: Damaged service wires or utility lines
checks: Stay far away from any downed wire and anything touching it.
Call the utility.
opts.stop: Assume every downed line is energized.
opts.pro: The utility repairs its lines; an electrician repairs damage on your side.

opts.label: From an appliance or tool
causes: A fault inside the appliance putting voltage on its case
A damaged cord
A missing or broken ground connection
checks: Don’t touch it again. Unplug it only if you can do so safely, or switch off its breaker.
opts.stop: CPSC: don’t use the appliance until it has been checked.
opts.pro: Have the appliance repaired or replaced, and an electrician check the outlet.

opts.label: From a faucet, tub, or other metal in the house
causes: A fault somewhere putting voltage on metal piping or fixtures
A grounding or bonding problem
checks: Stop using that fixture and keep others away from it.
opts.stop: Any shock, even a mild tingle, may be a warning of a dangerous wiring problem.
opts.pro: Call an electrician right away.

opts.label: From a switch or outlet plate
causes: A damaged device or exposed wiring
A missing or cracked cover plate
checks: Turn off that circuit at the panel unless it powers essential equipment.
opts.stop: Don’t use that outlet or switch.
opts.pro: Call an electrician.

opts.label: The neighbors too
causes: A utility outage
checks: Report it to your utility.
Unplug appliances and electronics to avoid damage from surges.
Keep the refrigerator and freezer closed.
Use flashlights, not candles.
opts.stop: If you use a generator, run it outside only, at least 20 feet from the house, and never plug it into a wall outlet.
opts.pro: The utility restores power. Call an electrician only if your own equipment was damaged.

opts.label: Only our house
causes: A tripped main breaker
A problem with your service wires or meter
checks: Check the main breaker in the panel.
Look outside, from a distance, for damaged service wires.
opts.stop: If the main breaker trips again, leave it off.
opts.pro: Call the utility about the service and meter; call an electrician for the panel.

opts.label: Wires are down outside
causes: Storm or accident damage to power lines
checks: Stay far away from the wires and anything touching them.
Call the utility.
opts.stop: Never go near a downed line. If one falls on your car, stay inside unless the car is on fire.
opts.pro: Only the utility handles downed lines.
